title: Tokens, Types and sizeof
quickIdea: sizeof answers a question about a type, not about a value: how many bytes the object occupies. In C it is an operator, settled before the program runs, and its result has the unsigned type size_t.
remember: GATE's convention unless a question says otherwise: char 1, short 2, int 4, float 4, double 8 bytes. A pointer is 4 bytes on a 32-bit build and 8 on a 64-bit build, and a question that needs a pointer's size states it.
sizeof is an operator, not a function: sizeof x is legal without parentheses, and the operand is not evaluated, so sizeof(i++) does not increment i.
sizeof(char) is 1 by definition, so sizeof of a char array equals its element count. sizeof("GATE") is 5, because a string literal carries its terminating NUL byte.
sizeof an array is (number of elements) x (element size). sizeof a pointer is the pointer's own size, whatever it points at.
sizeof a struct is at least the sum of its members and usually more, because of padding; sizeof a union is the size of its largest member, rounded up to the union's alignment.
'a' is a character constant of type int, so sizeof 'a' is 4. "a" is a string literal of type char[2], so sizeof "a" is 2. The two are not interchangeable.

example.prompt: On a machine where short is 2, float 4 and long 8 bytes, what is sizeof t for struct { short s[5]; union { float y; long z; } u; } t, ignoring alignment?
example.work: The member s is an array of 5 shorts, so 5 x 2 = 10 bytes. The member u is a union, so it is as large as its largest member, max(4, 8) = 8 bytes, and both of its members start at the same byte. The struct holds both members side by side, so its size is 10 + 8 = 18 bytes.
example.answer: 18 bytes. Swapping the union for a struct would give 10 + 4 + 8 = 22.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2000 asked exactly this struct-holding-a-union shape and the answer is 18. The exam's usual twist is the one-word change union to struct, which turns 18 into 22, or the sentence 'ignoring alignment' being dropped, which makes the answer depend on the compiler's alignment rules.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: What are sizeof("GATE") and sizeof s for char s[] = "GATE";?
variations.why: The literal is a five-byte array including its NUL, and the initialised array copies all five bytes. It tests the terminator that makes the 2000 question's arithmetic work.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: On a 64-bit build with 4-byte ints and 8-byte pointers, what does this print? void f(int a[10]) { printf("%zu", sizeof a); }
variations.answer: 8 - inside f the parameter is a pointer, not an array. The same sizeof at the caller, on int v[10], gives 40.
variations.why: The array-decay sizeof trap, which GATE has used inside larger questions rather than as a question of its own.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can sizeof(char) never be anything other than 1?
variations.answer: Because the C standard defines the unit in which sizeof counts as the size of a char, so 1 is true by definition and every other size is expressed in those units.
variations.why: Stops the habit of asking 'how big is a char on this machine' when the answer cannot vary.

trap.what: Reading sizeof of an array parameter as the array's size.
trap.why: A parameter declared int a[10] is adjusted by the compiler to int *a, so inside the function the name is a pointer and sizeof reports the pointer's size. The array's length is simply not available unless it is passed separately.
trap.counterexample: void f(int a[10]) { printf("%zu", sizeof a); } called on int v[10] prints 8 on a 64-bit build and 4 on a 32-bit one, never 40.

check.question: On the GATE convention (char 1, int 4), what does printf("%zu %zu", sizeof 'a', sizeof "a") print?
check.explanation: 'a' is a character constant whose type is int, so it is 4 bytes. "a" is a two-element char array holding 'a' and the NUL, so it is 2 bytes.
